sentence: Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at first, and any signs can build slowly over years.
note: NHS symptoms summary: many people have no symptoms at first; signs can build slowly over years.

sentence: The NHS lists feeling very tired, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss as the most common symptoms.
note: NHS: most common symptoms are tiredness, peeing more, thirst, unintended weight loss.

sentence: Other possible signs are blurred vision, wounds that heal slowly, and genital itching or repeated thrush.
note: NHS: blurred vision, slow-healing wounds, genital itching or recurrent thrush.

sentence: Because symptoms can be mild or missing, some people are found to have the condition during tests for something else.
note: Summary: some people are found to have it during tests for something else; many never notice signs.

sentence: The NHS describes prediabetes as blood glucose levels that are higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of diabetes.
note: Summary of NHS wording on prediabetes (page not individually returned; blended).

sentence: MedlinePlus explains that the pancreas at first makes extra insulin to make up for the body's cells not responding normally to it.
note: MedlinePlus: pancreas initially compensates by making more insulin.

sentence: Over time the body cannot make enough insulin, and blood glucose levels rise.
note: MedlinePlus: over time your body can't make enough insulin and blood glucose rises.

sentence: A GP can usually diagnose type 2 diabetes with a blood test and a urine test.
note: Summary of NHS symptoms/diagnosis page: a GP can usually diagnose via urine and blood test.

sentence: Guidance also uses HbA1c blood test results in diagnosis.
note: Summary: guidance also uses HbA1c levels (NICE-based criteria cited by an NHS document); no cut-off given here by design.

sentence: After diagnosis, NICE says there is a thorough check-up every year, called the annual review.
note: NICE: you will also have a thorough check-up every year, your annual review.

sentence: The review looks at complications and at whether treatment is working, and includes blood pressure, blood sugar and eye checks.
note: Diabetes UK care to expect: check-up to assess health, monitor complications, make sure treatment is working; blood pressure, blood sugar, eye checks.

sentence: It can also include a blood test for kidney function and a urine test for kidney disease.
note: Summary: you can expect a blood test for kidney function and a urine test for kidney disease (page attribution blended).

sentence: If kidney disease is found, treatment can be given to stop it getting worse.
note: Summary: if kidney disease is detected, treatment can be given to stop it getting worse.

sentence: A foot check looks at the risk of foot ulcers and at loss of feeling from nerve damage.
note: Summary: examination for foot ulcer risk and loss of sensation through nerve damage.

sentence: A foot check is needed even when no changes to the feet have been noticed.
note: Summary: you need a foot check even if you haven't noticed any changes.

sentence: Eye screening is usually a photograph of the back of the eye, taken to look for diabetic retinopathy, and it is often arranged separately from the annual review.
note: Summary: usually a photo of the back of the eye for retinopathy; often separate from the annual review.

sentence: The NHS describes treatment as lifestyle changes first, then medicines.
note: NHS treatment page: lifestyle changes first, then medicines.

sentence: Lifestyle steps include regular physical activity, losing weight for people who are overweight, stopping smoking and limiting alcohol.
note: NHS: activity, lose weight if overweight, stop smoking, limit alcohol.

sentence: A medicine called metformin is usually offered first.
note: NHS: you'll usually be offered a medicine called metformin first.

sentence: The NHS page notes that an SGLT2 inhibitor, which lets extra sugar leave the body in urine, is often given alongside metformin to people without other serious conditions.
note: NHS summary: people without other serious conditions are often given metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor, which lowers blood sugar by letting extra sugar leave in urine.

sentence: A weekly injection of a GLP-1 agonist may be offered to some people, such as those with a history of heart disease or with obesity, when other treatments are not enough.
note: NHS summary: weekly GLP-1 agonist injection may be offered to people with heart disease history or obesity when other treatments are not enough.

sentence: Other tablets such as gliclazide, sitagliptin or pioglitazone are also used.
note: NHS summary: other tablets such as gliclazide, sitagliptin or pioglitazone are also used.

sentence: The NHS says insulin is prescribed for type 2 diabetes if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range.
note: NHS insulin for type 2: needed if other medicines no longer work well enough to keep glucose in a healthy range.

sentence: Diabetes UK notes that some people can manage type 2 diabetes through healthy eating, being more active or losing weight.
note: Diabetes UK: some people can manage T2 through healthy eating, being more active or losing weight.

sentence: The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using soups and shakes, to eligible people in England who have type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.
note: NHS England page: low calorie total diet replacement incl. soups and shakes; eligible people with T2 and overweight/obesity.

sentence: Research cited by NHS England found that almost half of those on a low-calorie diet reached remission of their type 2 diabetes after one year.
note: Summary of NHS England page: almost half achieve remission after one year.

sentence: The NHS warns against very strict low-calorie diets without medical advice, especially for people taking insulin or other diabetes medicines.
note: NHS treatment page summary: warns against very strict low-calorie diets without medical advice.

sentence: Over time, high blood sugar can damage the blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums.
note: NHS complications summary: untreated high blood sugar over time affects these.

sentence: The NHS lists damage that can contribute to coronary heart disease and stroke, foot ulcers and infections that may sometimes lead to amputation, sight problems such as diabetic retinopathy, kidney problems and gum disease.
note: NHS complications page list.

sentence: The NHS says diabetes can reduce the blood supply to the feet and cause a loss of feeling.
note: Health problems page summary.

sentence: It also says that controlling blood sugar and having regular check-ups is the best way to lower the risk of complications.
note: Health problems page summary.

sentence: Very high blood glucose can lead to emergencies called diabetic ketoacidosis, when ketones build up in the blood, and HHS.
note: NHS complications summary: lack of insulin lets ketones build up (DKA); HHS also named; HHS not expanded in returned text.

sentence: The NHS says both can be life threatening.
note: Summary: both HHS and DKA can be life threatening.

sentence: For signs such as confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or vomiting with high blood glucose, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E.
note: Summary: confusion, breathlessness, extreme thirst/urination are reasons to call 999 or go to A&E; drowsiness and vomiting appear in a second summary line (blended).

sentence: For tingling, numbness, constipation or diarrhoea that could signal nerve damage, the NHS advises contacting a GP or diabetes nurse.
note: NHS: warning signs of nerve damage should prompt a call to a GP or diabetes nurse.

sentence: Blisters or cracked skin on the feet and worsening vision are also reasons to seek non-urgent advice, through a GP appointment.
note: NHS: blisters/cracked skin and worsening vision are reasons to seek non-urgent advice; route named per site rule.

sentence: NHS inform says a hot, red, swollen foot, new skin damage or new pain needs urgent contact with a podiatrist or GP, or NHS 111.
note: Summary: Scottish NHS guidance says contact a podiatrist or GP urgently for hot, red, swollen foot, new skin damage, change in shape, new pain; NHS 111 added as site signposting route.

sentence: UK guidance suggests a varied diet with plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains such as wholemeal bread and oats, and pulses such as chickpeas and lentils.
note: NHS Wales / NHS summary: varied diet with fruit, veg, wholegrains such as wholemeal bread and oats, pulses such as chickpeas and lentils.

sentence: The NHS notes that having diabetes increases the harmful effects of smoking.
note: Summary: the NHS notes diabetes increases the harmful effects of smoking.

sentence: The NHS says a free education course should be offered within a year of diagnosis.
note: Summary: NHS says you should be offered a free course within 1 year of diagnosis (page attribution blended).

sentence: The NHS advises checking the feet every day, with a yearly foot check by a clinician.
note: Health problems page summary: feet checked every day and every year by a clinician.

sentence: NHS Wales says people taking insulin for type 2 diabetes need to tell the DVLA, because of the risk of low blood sugar.
note: NHS 111 Wales: if taking insulin for T2 you need to tell DVLA because of risk of hypoglycaemia.

sentence: NHS England says contacting the DVLA may be needed if diabetes causes health problems or if there are low blood sugar episodes, known as hypos.
note: Summary: NHS England page says you may need to contact DVLA if diabetes causes health problems or hypos (page attribution blended; 'hypos' not defined in returned text).

sentence: Remission is possible for some people, according to NHS England.
note: NHS England remission page.

sentence: Its Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan to eligible people in England with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.
note: NHS England page.

note: Summary of NHS England page.

sentence: In type 2 diabetes the pancreas does not make enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to it.
note: Summary: in type 2 the pancreas doesn't produce enough insulin or cells don't react (blended; MedlinePlus and NHS inform).

sentence: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce any insulin.
note: Summary of the same sources.

sentence: One source adds that type 1 is an autoimmune condition, while type 2 is mainly influenced by lifestyle factors and genetics.
